Department of Botany, Faculty of Science, Charles University
Benátská 2, 128 41 Prague, Czech Republic
stencj@natur.cuni.cz
25 November 2026
Dear Editors,
please consider our manuscript “The law of large numbers explains stable conspecific pollen deposition” for publication as an Original Article in Annals of Botany.
A single pollinator visit delivers a very variable and usually small amount of pollen, yet the final pollen load on stigmas is often similar from year to year. We asked how this happens in Succisa pratensis, a generalist plant visited mostly by hoverflies, and whether the same holds for heterospecific pollen. Over three years we combined field observations of pollinator visits, pollen loads on pollinator bodies, single-visit deposition experiments and terminal stigma loads, and compared the field data with simple simulations built from the single-visit data.
Most of the variation in conspecific pollen on stigmas was among individual stigmas and plants, not among years or days. Single visits transferred only a small fraction of the pollen carried on the insect’s body, and the main pollinator groups did not differ in how much they deposited. When we let simulated stigmas accumulate randomly drawn single visits, they matched the observed conspecific loads well. Heterospecific pollen behaved differently: it was far higher than the simulations predicted in two years and dropped closer to the prediction in the year when S. pratensis flowered at high density.
Single-visit variability and stable stigma loads are both well known, but the link between them has been assumed rather than tested. The novelty of our study is that we measured the whole chain, from pollen on pollinators to single visits to final stigma loads, in one population over three years, and used it to test whether visit accumulation explains field loads. It does for conspecific but not for heterospecific pollen, which shows when factors beyond visit number, such as the flowering community, come into play.
In short, a plant with many generalist visitors can get a reliable conspecific pollen load simply because many visits average out, while heterospecific pollen depends on the surrounding flowering community. We think this fits well with the journal’s interest in pollination biology and the pathway from pollen transfer to reproduction.
The data and R code are archived on Figshare and will be made publicly available on acceptance. All authors have approved the manuscript, it is not under consideration elsewhere, and we declare no conflicts of interest.

title: The law of large numbers explains stable conspecific pollen deposition
text:
Summary
Animal-mediated pollen transfer is inherently stochastic: single-visit deposition (SVD) yields highly variable pollen loads, yet terminal pollen deposition (TPD), the final stigmatic load, often remains stable at the population level. The mechanisms buffering this visit-level unpredictability while mitigating reproductive interference from heterospecific pollen (HP) remain unresolved.
Using a three-year dataset (2022–2024) for Succisa pratensis, we combined variance partitioning of TPD with SVD experiments across dominant pollinator taxa and Monte Carlo simulations parameterized with empirical SVD and visitation frequency data.
Variance partitioning revealed that temporal shifts explained negligible variation in conspecific pollen (CP) deposition; the vast majority of variance occurred at the micro-scale among individual stigmas. SVD experiments confirmed that individual visits are highly stochastic and mechanically inefficient. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrated that accumulation across multiple visits effectively neutralises this unpredictability, translating into stable terminal CP loads. In contrast, HP accumulation was substantially more variable and depended on inter-annual variation in the floral neighbourhood.
Despite the mechanical unpredictability of individual pollinator visits, plants secure stable conspecific pollen receipt through the law of large numbers: visit accumulation converts stochastic single-visit events into reliable terminal loads. The potential for reproductive interference via heterospecific pollen depends largely on ecological context.
Keywords: Succisa pratensis; conspecific pollen deposition; heterospecific pollen; law of large numbers; plant–pollinator networks; reproductive interference; single-visit deposition

title: The law of large numbers explains stable conspecific pollen deposition
text:
Introduction
Pollen transfer by animal vectors is an inherently stochastic process (reviewed in Minnaar et al., 2019), where the number of pollen grains delivered during one pollinator visit (Single-Visit Deposition; SVD) exhibits high variance (Richards et al., 2009; King et al., 2013). Despite this micro-scale unpredictability, population-level studies demonstrate that terminal pollen deposition (TPD)—the final stigmatic pollen load prior to senescence—remains stable across multiple years (e.g., Fang et al., 2019, 2023). This stability provides reproductive assurance, driven by the accumulation of conspecific pollen (CP). Conversely, the receipt of heterospecific pollen (HP) from co-flowering species causes reproductive interference that negatively impacts plant fitness (Arceo-Gómez and Ashman, 2011). Determining how plants mitigate the high variance of SVD to secure CP receipt while mitigating HP accumulation remains a pending objective in pollination ecology.
At the SVD scale, the delivery of conspecific pollen is highly unpredictable, and pollen transfer is markedly inefficient. Even among legitimate pollinators, the quantity of pollen transferred fluctuates dramatically due to highly variable individual pollen loads (King et al., 2013; Freudenfeld et al., 2025). This stochasticity is compounded by taxon-specific differences in pollinator behaviour, such as grooming (Holmquist et al., 2012), insect morphological traits that drive pollen load composition (Cullen et al., 2021), pollen carryover dynamics across successive flower visits (Thomson and Plowright, 1980), and changing foraging decisions within the plant-pollinator community (Valdovinos, 2025). Because the quantity and purity of deposited pollen directly dictate ovule fertilization and plant fitness, this high SVD variance exerts strong selective pressure on plants. Consequently, plants must evolve ecological and morphological mechanisms to aggregate these variable events into a stable reproductive outcome (Richards et al., 2009).
To overcome the unpredictability of individual visits, some plants may rely on high visitation rates, accumulating a sufficient volume of visits to average out the variance of individual vectors and ensure reliable CP receipt. This is a direct consequence of the law of large numbers: as the number of independent stochastic events increases, their mean converges towards the expected value, such that the cumulative pollen load on a stigma becomes increasingly predictable even when individual visits are highly variable. The attraction of numerous pollinators is often facilitated by dense local floral displays (Vázquez, 2005; Janovský and Štenc, 2023) or rich flowering communities that draw diverse pollinator assemblages (Venjakob et al., 2016; Aguirre and Junker, 2024). However, accumulating pollinator visits within a network concurrently introduces the risk of reproductive interference in the form of HP received from other plant species sharing pollinators within the community (Morales and Traveset, 2008; Arceo-Gómez and Ashman, 2011). Co-flowering heterospecific neighbouring plant species act as sources of HP and alter the composition and fidelity of the pollinator assemblage visiting the focal plant (Lázaro et al., 2009; Ye et al., 2020). Therefore, plants face conflicting evolutionary pressures: maximizing visitation redundancy to ensure CP delivery while mitigating the associated influx of HP. High conspecific floral density serves as one density-dependent buffering mechanism, diluting the proportion of deposited HP by pulling pollinators from co-flowering neighbours (Arceo-Gómez et al., 2016).
Other mechanisms may be involved as well. For example, the density-dependent buffering can be significantly enhanced by the temporal stratification of plant-pollinator interactions within the community (Stone et al., 1998; Schwarz et al., 2021). For example, the diurnal pollen release schedules previously observed in Succisa pratensis allow the plant to establish temporal dominance by attracting pollinators primarily early in the day (Štenc et al., 2023). By releasing pollen and attracting vectors before co-flowering competitors do, a plant can secure substantial CP delivery prior to the accumulation of heterogeneous pollen loads on shared vectors, functioning as a form of temporal specialisation (Brosi, 2016). This temporal stratification ensures that the highest-frequency visits occur within a specific time window, mitigating the subsequent accumulation of HP (Schwarz et al., 2021; Štenc et al., 2023).
While the variability of individual visits and the theoretical frameworks for pollen accumulation are well known, empirical studies rarely measure these processes across multiple scales in a natural system. In this study, we evaluate pollen transfer using a three-year dataset (2022–2024) for the highly visited plant Succisa pratensis. We address the following objectives: (1) to quantify the hierarchical variance in pollen deposition across years, days, individual plants, and individual stigmas; (2) to compare the mechanistic efficiency of CP and HP transfer across dominant vector taxa at the SVD scale; (3) to mathematically test whether visitation redundancy drives stable CP deposition using Monte Carlo simulations; and (4) to determine how year-to-year changes in local conspecific floral abundance influence the accumulation of HP. We hypothesise that despite the high variability of individual generalist visits, S. pratensis achieves stable CP deposition because its high local floral abundance and early morning pollen release (Štenc et al., 2023, 2025) evolved as traits that buffer the plant against unpredictable single-visit deliveries.






Figure 1: Conceptual diagram of the proposed pollen deposition framework. Individual pollinator visits deliver highly variable conspecific (CP) and heterospecific (HP) pollen loads to Succisa pratensis stigmas (left; Single-Visit Deposition, SVD). The accumulation of many independent visits over the stigma lifespan (centre) filters micro-scale variance through the law of large numbers, producing stable terminal CP loads (right). In contrast, HP accumulation remains ecologically context-dependent and is partially buffered by high conspecific floral density.

title: The law of large numbers explains stable conspecific pollen deposition
text:
Materials and Methods

Study system
Our observations were conducted in a semi-natural grassland community characterised by a high abundance of flowering plants and a diverse pollinator community dominated by hoverflies. The study site, “K Handrkovu”, is located near the village of Vernýřov, Central Bohemia, Czech Republic (49.8466° N, 15.1498° E). The site can be classified as a mosaic of moist-to-mesophilic and eutrophic-to-mesotrophic grasslands, supporting more than 50 entomogamous plant species that flower in late summer each year (Janovský et al., 2013). Fieldwork was conducted from 2022 to 2024 during the peak of S. pratensis flowering activity (15–19 August, 13–20 August, and 11–18 August, respectively).
Succisa pratensis, our focal plant species, maintains a relatively large and stable population at our study site. It is frequently visited by a wide spectrum of pollinators—especially hoverflies (Figure 2)—which feed on both its pollen and nectar. Important traits related to its pollination include distinctive open inflorescences accessible to most pollinators, protandry to prevent self-pollination (Bartoš et al., 2020), and a diurnal pollen release schedule occurring in the morning hours (Štenc et al., 2023).
 








Figure 2: A) Stigma of Succisa pratensis with several pollen morphotypes; B) Pollinator (Eristalis sp.) on a flower of S. pratensis, highlighting pollen visible on the pollinator’s body; C) Detail of an anther with visible pollen grains of S. pratensis; D) Detail of a stigma of S. pratensis with visible deposited pollen grains.







Plant-Pollinator Interactions and Plant Abundance
Following the established protocol for this study locality (Janovský et al., 2013), we collected data on pollinator visitation activity in 93 permanent plots arranged in a semi-regular grid, spaced 20 m apart across the study site. All plots were permanently marked with a metal nail, recovered using a metal detector, and visibly marked prior to the sampling event each year. Within the plots, we recorded flowering plant abundance and all interactions of flower-visiting pollinators with flowering S. pratensis, as well as with other plant species in the surrounding community. To avoid pseudoreplication, all flowers within a plot were surveyed only once per individual sampling event. All interactions occurring during the survey moment were recorded, lasting up to five minutes per plot. Each plot was surveyed at least twenty times during a sampling period spanning 5–10 consecutive days at the peak of flowering (mid-August) each year. For this study, we utilised interactions recorded during the main diurnal period of pollinator activity (07:00–19:00). We recorded only the pollinators that made contact with the reproductive organs of the visited plant, counting each individual pollinator only once. Finally, we computed standardised interaction rates (total number of interactions per plot survey) for pollinators visiting S. pratensis from 2022 to 2024, and compared the distribution of interaction rates for the specific group of pollinators visiting S. pratensis against those visiting all other plant species.
To determine plant abundance, we surveyed the plots twice during each sampling event to control for potential phenological shifts; for this study, we used the average plant abundance per sampling event. To record abundance, we divided each plot into 64 individual cells using a string grid gently placed over the plot. Within each cell, we either counted the flowering stalks or recorded the presence/absence of flowering plants, depending on the species.


Pollen Load
In 2024, we investigated the number of pollen grains carried on the pollinators’ bodies. Foraging pollinators visiting S. pratensis inflorescences were captured with an entomological net and euthanised immediately. Following Beattie (1971), we swabbed pollen grains from one half of each pollinator’s body (randomly selecting the left or right side) using a small block of Fuchsin jelly. Captured pollinators were subsequently stored in 70% ethanol. On the same day, we produced semi-permanent slides by melting the Fuchsin jelly onto a microscope slide using a heating pad, adding a coverslip, and sealing it with nail polish. We later counted and identified all pollen grains using a light microscope, sorting them into conspecific S. pratensis pollen and heterospecific pollen (HP) from other plant species.


Single-Visit Deposition (SVD)
To estimate the pollinator single-visit deposition (SVD), we followed protocols adapted from previous studies (King et al., 2013; Valverde et al., 2019). To prevent prior pollinator access, we enclosed selected inflorescences in fine-mesh tulle bags before the plants entered the male phase and opened their anthers. Once a plant entered the female phase with receptive stigmas, we removed the bag and observed the inflorescence until the arrival of the first pollinator. Pollinators were allowed to visit only one flower within the inflorescence, after which we immediately collected its stigma into a microcentrifuge tube containing 70% ethanol. If a pollinator visited multiple flowers, we collected only the first visited stigma and removed the others from the plant. The SVD experiments were conducted in 2022, 2023 and 2024.


Terminal Pollen Deposition (TPD) on Stigma
To determine terminal pollen deposition (TPD), we collected stigmas from flowers with visibly senesced or absent corollas, indicative of the late flowering stage (pers. obs.). Each year, we collected 3 randomly selected stigmas per flowerhead to account for intra-inflorescence variability, and from 30 randomly selected individuals from the population per day. In 2022 and 2023, we collected samples during only one day, in 2024 we sampled stigmas during 6 days, following the same 3 stigma per flowerhead and 30 plant individual design.
We placed the collected stigmas onto microscope slides and allowed the ethanol to evaporate on a heating pad. Subsequently, we applied 1 µL of 10% KOH and allowed the samples to dry, followed by 3 µL of 3% hydrogen peroxide. After another drying period, we added 13 µL of 8% acetic acid. Once completely dry, we applied 5 µL of a dye solution (safranin, water, and glycerol), covered the samples with a coverslip, applied gentle, even pressure to squash the stigma, and sealed the edges with nail polish to create semi-permanent samples. We discarded samples which were destroyed during the processing or were insufficient for pollen counting. Pollen grains were counted and identified under a light microscope at 400× magnification. Based on the pollen morphology (size, shape and ornamentation), we distinguished conspecific (Succisa pratensis) pollen grains from heterospecific pollen grains (HP).


Statistical Analysis
All statistical analyses were performed in R (version 4.3.3; R Core Team (2024)). To systematically evaluate pollen transfer dynamics across hierarchical scales, our analyses were structured into four primary components: (1) community stability and visitation dynamics, (2) single-visit transfer efficiency, (3) variance partitioning of terminal pollen deposition (TPD), and (4) mathematical simulations of visitation redundancy.

Community Stability and Visitation Dynamics
To assess the temporal consistency of the local ecological network, we calculated the Morisita-Horn similarity index for both the pollinator visitation spectra and the co-flowering plant community across the three study years. Differences in standardised visitation rates (total interactions per plot) and per-capita visitation rates (interactions per focal plant) across years were analysed using Kruskal-Wallis rank-sum tests, followed by post hoc Dunn’s tests with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate corrections. Furthermore, to formalise the density-dependent dilution effect, we fitted a log-log linear regression evaluating how per-capita visitation rates scaled with local S. pratensis plot abundance.


Single-Visit Deposition (SVD)
To evaluate micro-scale mechanical transfer, pollinators were categorised into dominant morpho-groups (e.g., Eristalis spp., Helophilus spp., Bombus spp.). Differences in both conspecific pollen (CP) delivery and heterospecific pollen (HP) carryover during a single visit were tested across these taxa using Kruskal-Wallis rank-sum tests.


Variance Partitioning
To identify the exact spatial and temporal scales driving unpredictability in terminal stigmatic pollen loads, we applied Variance Components Analysis (VCA) using Linear Mixed Models (LMMs). Prior to modelling, pollen counts were square-root transformed to stabilise variance and approximate normality, as confirmed by residual diagnostic plots (‘Residuals vs. Fitted’ and ‘Normal Q-Q’, see Section S1). Because fine-scale daily data were exclusively available for the 2024 season, we constructed two complementary LMMs to prevent rank deficiency: an inter-annual model spanning 2022–2024 (1 | year / plant_id), and an intra-annual model restricted to 2024 (1 | date / plant_id). The statistical significance of these hierarchical random effects (Year, Date, and Plant) was evaluated using Likelihood Ratio Tests.
Furthermore, to test how HP accumulation scales with CP receipt, and whether this relationship shifted during the high-density anomaly of 2024, we aggregated pollen counts to the plant level. We fitted a linear model testing the interaction between transformed CP and Year (sqrt(mean_HP) ~ sqrt(mean_CP) * Year; see Section S2 for model selection and Section S3 for diagnostics). Differences in the rates of HP accumulation across years were subsequently quantified using pairwise slope contrasts via estimated marginal means.


Monte Carlo Simulation of Visitation Redundancy
To test whether visitation redundancy mathematically drives stable pollen deposition, we constructed a Monte Carlo bootstrapping simulation. Because pollinator morphology and mechanical transfer efficiency are functionally consistent traits, we pooled all single-visit deposition (SVD) data across the three study years to create a single, highly robust global pool of vector deposition profiles. This allowed us to mathematically isolate the effect of the plant’s changing floral density while holding vector baseline deposition constant.
We parameterised the simulation independently for each study year (2022–2024). For a given year, we estimated the average required visitation rate by dividing the empirical mean of conspecific pollen (CP) on that year’s stigmas by the mean CP of the global SVD pool. We then generated 10,000 virtual stigmas per year, randomly sampling (with replacement) from the global SVD pool based on that year’s specific visitation rate.
Finally, we evaluated the fit of the simulated null models against our true field observations. Because the large sample size of the simulation (N = 10,000) renders traditional two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) p-values hypersensitive to trivial biological deviations—such as physical stigma saturation limits—we focused on the K-S D-statistic to quantify the maximum distributional divergence as a measure of effect size. Furthermore, to provide a robust and intuitive measure of simulation accuracy independent of sample size, we calculated the Overlapping Coefficient (OVL; Pastore and Calcagnì (2019)). The OVL quantifies the exact proportion of area shared between the empirical and simulated probability density curves, providing a direct metric of functional overlap between the theoretical null model and field reality.

title: The law of large numbers explains stable conspecific pollen deposition
text:
Results
Across the three-year study period (2022–2024), we collected and analysed a total of 693 terminal-stage stigmas from 273 individual Succisa pratensis plants to evaluate terminal pollen deposition (TPD). We sampled 84 stigmas in 2022, 89 stigmas in 2023, and 520 stigmas in 2024, with collections conducted over 6 consecutive days. To quantify micro-scale transfer dynamics and vector efficiency, we captured pollen from 300 individual visitors of S. pratensis to assess body pollen loads (Table S1), and we sampled 124 controlled single-visit deposition (SVD) events on virgin stigmas (Table S2). Finally, we recorded 2998 individual plant-pollinator interactions during standardised focal plot observations (Table S3). Detailed descriptions of the individual results follow.

Coefficient of Variation and Variance Partitioning of TPD
To quantify the unpredictability of pollen transport, we compared the Coefficient of Variation (CV) across functional transport compartments (Figure 3). Conspecific pollen (CP) exhibited high variability on pollinator bodies (CV = 129%) and in SVDs (CV = 206%). However, at the TPD stage, the variability decreased considerably (CV = 69%). Conversely, heterospecific pollen (HP) remained relatively variable across all compartments, from vector bodies (CV = 264%) through to final stigmatic loads (CV = 147%; see Section S7 for raw data distribution). The inter-annual variability of TPD remained relatively stable across years for CP (CVs ranging from 66% to 73%), but the variability of HP increased in 2024 (CV = 125%, Figure 3).
Hierarchical variance partitioning further confirmed the micro-scale nature of this stochasticity in TPD (Figure 4; Tables S4 and S5). For CP, temporal phenology (years and days) explained only a small proportion of the variation; instead, the vast majority of depositional variance occurred at the micro-spatial scale, driven by differences among individual plants (15%) and individual stigmas (82%). Variance partitioning and subsequent likelihood ratio tests (Table S6) revealed that HP deposition was significantly driven by temporal shifts at the macro-scale (\(\chi^2 = 32.39, p < 0.001\)) and by spatial variation among individual plants nested within the year (\(\chi^2 = 104.73, p < 0.001\)).
Notably, intra-annual analysis of the 2024 season showed that daily temporal variation was not a significant driver of either CP or HP deposition (\(\chi^2 = 1.32, p = 0.517\) for CP; \(\chi^2 = 0.19, p = 0.663\) for HP). Instead, variance during the 2024 season was heavily driven by differences among individual plants (\(\chi^2 = 126.53, p < 0.001\)), suggesting that plant-level traits or highly localised micro-spatial effects dictate heterospecific pollen transfer more than daily phenological shifts.
 








Figure 3: Coefficient of Variation (CV) and Mean of Conspecific (CP) and Heterospecific (HP) pollen counts across different compartments and years. A) Inter-compartmental variability (CV) comparing pollen loads on pollinator bodies (Body), single-visit deposition (SVD), and final Terminal Pollen Deposition (TPD). B) Interannual variability (CV) of TPD across 2022–2024. C) Mean pollen counts (± SE) across the three compartments, highlighting the significant drop from body loads to SVD. D) Mean TPD (± SE) across the three study years.





 








Figure 4: Pollen Deposition Model and Variance Partitioning. A) Back-transformed predictions (± 95% CI) from a linear model fitted to square-root transformed plant-level mean pollen counts (sqrt(mean_HP) ~ sqrt(mean_CP) * Year), showing the accumulation of Heterospecific Pollen (HP) relative to Conspecific Pollen (CP) across three years (2022–2024; points denote individual plant means). The dashed grey line indicates the 1:1 relationship, illustrating that CP accumulates substantially faster than HP. B) Hierarchical variance partitioning of square-root transformed terminal pollen loads (Linear Mixed-Effects Models), showing the percentage of variance in HP and CP explained by Year, Plant, and individual Stigma (Inter-Annual, 2022–2024) and by Date, Plant, and individual Stigma (Intra-Annual, 2024).

Pollen Load and Single-Visit Deposition (SVD)
To evaluate the mechanical efficiency of pollen transfer, we compared the total pollen loads carried on vector bodies to the amounts of pollen successfully deposited on stigmas during single-visit depositions (SVD). Pollinators carried substantial pollen loads (Mean Body CP = 147.8 (SD = 393.6); Mean Body HP = 478.8 (SD = 1102.2)). However, per-visit mechanical transfer was remarkably inefficient. Only a minute fraction of the available body load, approximately 2.3% for CP and 0.1% for HP, was successfully deposited onto a receptive stigma during a single floral visit.
To determine if specific pollinator taxa drive the depositional variance observed across the network, we compared single-visit depositions (SVD) across the dominant floral visitor morphogroups (e.g., Eristalis spp., Helophilus spp., Bombus spp.). Kruskal-Wallis rank-sum tests revealed no significant differences among pollinator taxa in the amount of conspecific pollen deposited during a single visit (\(H_3 = 1.59, p = 0.661\)). Similarly, there were no significant differences across taxa in the deposition of heterospecific pollen per visit (\(H_3 = 5.20, p = 0.158\)). These results indicate that per-visit pollen transfer efficiency and heterospecific pollen carryover may be highly stochastic but functionally equivalent across the studied pollinator morphogroups. Consequently, the terminal stigmatic pollen loads received by S. pratensis are not dictated by the taxonomic identity or morphological specialisation of its visitors, but purely by the cumulative frequency of their visits.
 








Figure 5: Distribution of pollen loads carried by pollinators and deposited during single visits. A–B) Histograms showing the highly skewed distribution of Conspecific (CP) and Heterospecific (HP) pollen grains present on the bodies of captured pollinators. C–D) Corresponding distributions of CP and HP successfully deposited onto virgin stigmas during controlled single-visit deposition (SVD) experiments, demonstrating the high stochasticity and low efficiency of single transfer events.







Pollinator Visitation Spectra and Co-flowering Community Stability
To assess the temporal stability of the pollinator visitation spectra of S. pratensis (Figure 6) and the co-flowering plant community, we compared species composition across years using the Morisita-Horn similarity index (Horn, 1966). The pollinator spectra showed high compositional overlap across the years, ranging from 0.78 to 0.96 similarity. The flowering plant community composition showed lower overlap, ranging from 0.69 to 0.71.
The pollinator visitation spectra of S. pratensis (Table S3, Figure 6 A) was dominated by large hoverflies, namely Eristalis tenax (n = 1,127, 37.6%), Eristalis interrupta (n = 403, 13.4%), Helophilus trivittatus (n = 346, 11.5%), Eristalis pertinax (n = 138, 4.6%), and Helophilus pendulus (n = 105, 3.5%). Other frequent visitors included Zygaena sp. (n = 129, 4.3%), Apis mellifera (n = 98, 3.3%), and Bombus lapidarius (n = 71, 2.4%), with all other taxa each accounting for less than 2.2% of the total recorded visits.
 








Figure 6: Plant and pollinator community composition and temporal stability. A) Relative abundance of major pollinator functional groups visiting Succisa pratensis across the three study years. B) Relative floral abundance of the surrounding co-flowering plant community. C) Temporal stability of the pollinator community measured using the Morisita-Horn overlap index across consecutive years. D) Temporal stability of the floral community similarity, indicating high consistency in the background community over time.







Floral Density and Visitations
Despite the increase in S. pratensis abundance in 2024, sampling-effort-standardised visitation rates per plot and per plant did not differ significantly between years.








Figure 7: Spatial distribution and temporal abundance of Succisa pratensis and its pollinators (2022-2024). A) Spatial map showing the distribution and relative size of plots with Succisa presence. B) Total floral abundance of Succisa pratensis recorded across the study sites per year. C) Boxplots showing differences in standardized pollinator visitation rates to Succisa pratensis across the three years, with individual data points overlaid.







Monte Carlo Simulation: The Interannual Variance Filter
The year-by-year Monte Carlo simulation confirmed that visitation redundancy effectively neutralises micro-scale stochasticity for conspecific pollen (CP) across all measured years in the TPD. Regardless of the study year, the random additive accumulation of SVDs from the global vector pool successfully recreated the stable mean CP loads observed in the field (e.g., 2024 Simulated CP Mean: 26.8; Observed CP Mean: 27.4). While the two-sample K-S tests flagged mathematical divergences (\(p < 0.001\)) due to the hypersensitivity of a 10,000-iteration model to biological saturation limits, the tight convergence of the central tendencies and the functional overlap of the distributions (D-statistics ranging from 0.103 to 0.166) demonstrate that visitation frequency alone acts as a robust mathematical filter, effectively translating single-visit variance into stable CP deposition.
Conversely, for heterospecific pollen (HP), the simulation’s accuracy varied sharply between years, revealing that HP accumulation is governed by environmental context rather than simple mechanical redundancy. If generalist vectors deposit mixed pollen loads based strictly on their baseline single-visit profiles, the null model dictates that stigmas should accumulate a low, normalised baseline load of HP (3.4 to 4.5 grains). In standard-density years (2022 and 2023), empirical stigmas accumulated HP loads that exceeded this mathematical expectation by more than tenfold (e.g., 2023 Observed HP: 50.4 vs. Simulated: 3.4), resulting in severe structural divergence from the null model (\(D > 0.77\)). Crucially, during the increased density of S. pratensis in 2024, this neighbourhood-driven accumulation declined. The observed HP dropped to 9.6 grains, forcing the empirical distribution significantly closer to the mechanical baseline (\(D = 0.265\)). Because vector mechanical efficiency was held constant in our simulation, this interannual shift confirms that while standard-density years suffer heavy reproductive interference from shared networks, the increased conspecific floral abundance in 2024 actively mitigated HP accumulation, suppressing it back toward the mechanical minimum.

title: The law of large numbers explains stable conspecific pollen deposition
text:
Discussion
Generalist pollination systems operate under high micro-scale unpredictability (Richards et al., 2009; King et al., 2013), yet population-level conspecific pollen deposition often remains stable (Fang et al., 2019). Our results demonstrate that plants subject to highly stochastic single-visit pollen delivery achieve stable terminal conspecific deposition simply through mathematical averaging. Visitation redundancy neutralizes conspecific variance. Variance partitioning revealed that CP receipt is stable against inter-annual shifts, restricting variance in TPD almost entirely to individual stigmas and plants. The Monte Carlo simulation supports this mechanism, demonstrating that the statistical law of large numbers translates highly variable single visits into population-level CP stability. This stabilizing effect is asymmetric; while CP receipt is buffered by visitation frequency, HP accumulation remains highly variable and environment-dependent (Arceo-Gómez et al., 2016).
Achieving stable TPD through visitation redundancy directly influences plant fitness and sexual selection. Succisa pratensis possesses a single ovule; successful fertilization theoretically requires one viable grain. Accumulating CP loads that vastly exceed this minimum requirement shifts the reproductive bottleneck from the pollinator’s body to the plant’s stigmas. High-volume CP deposition triggers intense pollen-pollen competition (Minnaar et al., 2019). By securing excessive CP loads despite highly variable individual deliveries, high visitation rates act as a mechanism to sample multiple pollen donors, enabling post-pollination selection based on pollen competitive ability (Hildesheim et al., 2019; Madjidian et al., 2020). The micro-scale unpredictability of individual visits potentially acts as a selective pressure driving floral traits that maximize pollinator attraction and visitation redundancy.
Single-visit deposition (SVD) analysis revealed no significant differences in CP or HP transfer across dominant pollinator taxa. Functionally, a single visit from a Bombus bee was indistinguishable from a visit by an Eristalis syrphid fly (Figure 5 C). While previous frameworks emphasize morphological specialization, our data show that the extreme stochasticity of individual visits overrides taxonomic differences in mechanical transfer efficiency. Reproductive success in this system is driven by vector abundance rather than morphological specialization. These results support recent findings that large hoverflies and bees exhibit functional equivalence in pollen transfer capacity (Freudenfeld et al., 2025).
Unlike the mathematically determined stability of CP, HP deposition is context-dependent and exhibits high inter-annual variability. The extent of HP contamination represents reproductive interference driven by environmental fluctuations rather than mechanical redundancy. HP accumulation is not successfully predicted by simple visitation models because pollinator fidelity fluctuates dynamically based on co-flowering phenology and local floral density. In years with increased density of co-flowering heterospecific neighbors, the attractive pull of competitors alters the fidelity of shared generalist pollinators (Morales and Traveset, 2008; Flanagan et al., 2010), driving interspecific transitions and increasing HP loads (Bell et al., 2005). To mitigate environmentally driven HP accumulation, focal plants are under selective pressure to employ spatial or temporal isolation traits. High conspecific floral density acts as a spatial buffer against HP transfer, while diurnal pollen release schedules establish temporal dominance over shared vectors.
Nevertheless, our study possesses limitations that must be addressed in future research. First, while we found no significant differences among morphological groups of pollinators in their single-visit pollen deposition (SVD), this lack of difference may be partly due to the stochastic nature of individual depositions, potentially requiring more sampling to detect the subtle effects of pollinator traits on pollen deposition (Ne’eman et al., 2010; King et al., 2013). Second, our SVD methodology provides an evidence of pollen transfer, but it does not explicitly track the previous foraging history or complex pollen carryover dynamics of individual pollinators prior to capture (Thomson and Plowright, 1980; Cullen et al., 2021). Consequently, while our data demonstrate that multiple SVD events mathematically aggregate into stable CP loads, we currently lack the genetic parentage data, as well as the data on stigma receptivity and pollen tube germination required to confirm whether this high visitation redundancy translates into a highly diverse pollen donor pool and subsequent pollen-pollen competition along the pathway to paternity (Karron and Mitchell, 2012; Minnaar et al., 2019; Stavert et al., 2020).
The fact that the pollen deposited on stigmas is the result of multiple SVD events suggests that the composition of pollen competing for ovule fertilization is formed by pollen from several distinct donors. This has direct implications for pollen-pollen competition, male reproductive success, and population genetic variability (Bernasconi et al., 2004). A remaining question is whether the pollen delivered during the first visits has a decisive competitive advantage over later-delivered pollen (Lankinen and Madjidian, 2011), or if this advantage is limited by the timing of stigma receptivity acting as a synchronized starting gate (Herrero, 2003). Beyond this micro-scale pollen-pollen competition, the macro-scale genetic implications of stochastic visits remain unknown. Because vector foraging behavior and heterospecific carryover fluctuate with local floral density (Arceo-Gómez and Ashman, 2011), the hidden donor-acceptor mating network may undergo radical year-to-year rewiring (CaraDonna et al., 2017). Determining whether these dynamic micro-competitive mechanisms and macro-level network shifts represent a generalizable feature of plant-pollinator systems remains an open question for future ecological and evolutionary research.

Conclusions
Stable pollen transfer in generalized networks is driven by distinct, scale-dependent mechanisms. While individual generalist vectors exhibit extreme depositional stochasticity, plants achieve reliable conspecific pollen receipt through the law of large numbers: the accumulation of many independent, variable visits converges on a stable mean load, providing reproductive assurance without requiring morphological specialization of individual vectors. Visitation redundancy alone is functionally insufficient to prevent reproductive interference from the co-flowering community, and variations in community composition influence HP transfer. The mitigation of heterospecific pollen accumulation then possibly relies on several mechanisms such as the local spatial structure of the focal population and pollinator temporal specialization (Brosi, 2016; Štenc et al., 2025).

8.2 Data Description
These datasets contain empirical data collected to investigate the mechanisms linking pollinator visitation networks to stigmatic pollen deposition on Succisa pratensis. The study investigates how community-level network structure (specialization, interaction evenness) and single-visit pollen deposition stochastics scale to population-level pollination outcomes across three years (2022-2024).
The provided files are: - pollen_deposition.csv: Total pollen loads on stigmas collected from the field. - SVD.csv: Single-visit deposition experimental data. - network_metrics.csv: Aggregated yearly metrics constructed from three primary data sources: 1. Plant-pollinator visitation networks: Used to calculate network-level specialization (\(H_2'\)) and species-level specialization/interaction evenness for Succisa pratensis using the bipartite R package. 2. Stigmatic pollen deposition: Used to calculate the linear slope of Conspecific (CP) vs. Heterospecific (HP) pollen accumulation, and mean HP loads. 3. Floral abundance transects: Used to calculate the mean Succisa pratensis abundance per plot and total community floral abundance. - interaction_data_all_22_24.csv: Full plant-pollinator visitation observation data for the entire community across all years. - interaction_data_Succisa_22_24.csv: Subset of the visitation data containing only observations for Succisa pratensis. - plant_abundance_22_24.csv: Floral abundance transect data for all plots across years. - pollen_load_and_guts_2024_Succisa_pratensis.csv: Raw pollen load and gut content data for individual pollinators.

title: The law of large numbers explains stable conspecific pollen deposition
text:
Abstract

Background and Aims Animal-mediated pollen transfer is inherently stochastic: single-visit deposition (SVD) yields highly variable pollen loads, yet terminal pollen deposition (TPD), the final stigmatic load, often remains stable at the population level. How generalized plants buffer this visit-level unpredictability while mitigating reproductive interference from heterospecific pollen (HP) remains unresolved.
Methods Using a three-year dataset (2022–2024) for Succisa pratensis, we combined hierarchical variance partitioning of TPD across temporal and micro-spatial scales with pollinator body-load quantification, controlled SVD experiments across dominant pollinator morphogroups, and Monte Carlo simulations parameterized with empirical SVD and visitation data.
Key Results Variance partitioning revealed that inter-annual and daily shifts explained negligible variation in conspecific pollen (CP) deposition; nearly all variance occurred at the micro-scale among individual stigmas and plants. SVD experiments showed that individual visits are highly stochastic, mechanically inefficient, and functionally equivalent across dominant hoverfly and bumblebee morphogroups. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrated that visit accumulation neutralises single-visit unpredictability, reproducing stable terminal CP loads. Conversely, HP accumulation diverged sharply from the random-visit null model across years and declined substantially under high conspecific floral density.
Conclusions Despite extreme mechanical unpredictability in individual generalist visits, plants secure reliable conspecific pollen receipt through the law of large numbers: visit accumulation filters stochastic single-visit deliveries into stable terminal loads without requiring pollinator morphological specialization. In contrast, reproductive interference via heterospecific pollen is governed by floral neighbourhood context and mitigated by conspecific floral density and temporal pollen presentation.

Key words: Conspecific pollen deposition, heterospecific pollen, law of large numbers, plant–pollinator networks, pollen transfer mechanics, reproductive interference, single-visit deposition, Succisa pratensis.

J.Š. planned and designed the research, developed the methodology, and acquired funding. J.Š., M.F., P.Š., E.M., J.H., M.M., T.R., H.P., E.H. and Z.J. performed fieldwork and collected data. J.Š. analysed and interpreted the data. J.Š. and M.F. wrote the manuscript. M.F. and P.Š. contributed substantially to writing, and all authors reviewed and edited the manuscript.
